qa.question:
Would the board and management provide unitholders with greater clarity on the 
following operational and financial matters? Specifically: 
 
(i) 
PLQ Mall: Has the mall performed up to management’s expectations since 
the acquisition, and what return does management expect to generate from 
the reconfiguration of approximately 16,000 sq ft of retail space?  
 
(ii) 
Milan: While Buildings 1 and 2 are fully leased to Sky Italia through January 2033, 
Building 3 has been configured for multi-tenancy with a committed occupancy of 
approximately 51%. What was the average actual occupancy of Building 3 
during FY2026? Does the manager expect to market all three buildings as a 
portfolio, or would it consider divesting Buildings 1 and 2 separately given 
their long-term lease to Sky Italia? 
 
(iii) 
Grange House: The 3,000-capacity purpose-built entertainment venue next to 
313@somerset is expected to be operationally ready in mid-2027. Can 
management elaborate on the business and revenue model of the venue? 
 
(iv) 
Rental reversion and tenant retention rate: Has the manager benchmarked 
the 11.7% rental reversion for retail and tenant retention rate of 70.8% 
over an extended leasing cycle?

As at 30 June 2026, the REIT’s gross borrowings stood at $1.71 billion, with aggregate 
leverage ratio at 38.9%. While the interest coverage ratio improved from 1.6 times to 2.1 
times, it remains relatively low. The REIT reported a weighted average cost of debt of 2.75% 
per annum, down from 3.46% a year ago.   
 
(i) 
Weighted average cost of debt: The reported average cost of debt excludes 
amortisation of debt-related transaction costs (and other fees). What is the all-
in weighted average cost of debt? When evaluating refinancing, new debt or 
other funding options, does the manager assess funding costs on an all-in 
basis, including transaction costs, fees and other financing-related 
expenses? 
 
(ii) 
Perpetual securities: The REIT redeemed $200 million of Perpetual Securities 
Series 001, which carried a coupon of 4.20%, while issuing $120 million of new 
Perpetual Securities Series 004 at a higher coupon rate of 4.28%. Can the board 
explain the role of perpetual securities within the REIT's overall capital 
management strategy? In particular, how does the manager assess the 
economic cost of perpetual securities against bank borrowings? To what 
extent did the manager choose to issue the Series 004 perpetual securities 
and not to take up additional bank borrowings so as to maintain the REIT’s 
aggregate leverage?

At the close of the REIT’s preferential offering on 18 March 2026, valid acceptances 
amounted to 53.05% of the units available for subscription, with a further 9.14% of units 
taken up through excess applications. 
 
(Source: 
https://links.sgx.com/FileOpen/Results%20of%20Preferential%20Offering_Final.ashx?Ap
p=Announcement&FileID=880048) 
 
(i) 
Has the manager undertaken a post-mortem analysis of the preferential 
offering to understand the low level of valid acceptances? In particular, 
what did the manager learn from the take-up to indicate about unitholders' 
willingness to commit additional capital to the REIT, and did the manager 
identify any concerns relating to the terms of the offering, pricing, 
underlying asset or the track record of the manager? 
 
(ii) 
How did the manager come to believe that a non-renounceable preferential 
offering was the most appropriate method of raising capital in the 
circumstances? How did the independent directors assess the impact on 
unitholders who were unwilling or unable to commit additional capital? 
Also, how did the independent directors satisfy themselves that the terms 
and structure of the preferential offering appropriately balanced the REIT's 
funding requirements with the interests of existing unitholders? 
 
Separately, the REIT also conducted a private placement in November 2025 in which new 
units were issued at $0.602 per unit, compared with the last reported net asset value per 
unit of $0.75, representing a discount of 20%. The private placement raised gross proceeds 
of no less than $270 million to support the acquisition of PLQ Mall. 
 
(iii) 
Can the independent directors provide unitholders with justification why 
placing out new units at a 20% discount to acquire an asset at 2.2% discount 
to its appraised value is in the interest of minority unitholders?

As shown in the consolidated statement of cash flow below, contract assets increased by

(Source: company annual report; emphasis added)  
 
The annual report also shows that trade receivables turnover days increased from 52 days

to 80 days. 

(i) 
What guidance has the board given to management to improve cash 
conversion and align operating cash flow more closely with reported 
profits? What measurable targets has the board set for working capital 
efficiency, and by when does it expect operating cash flow to become 
consistently positive? 
 
(ii) 
Specifically for contract assets which increased by $15.0 million, what were 
the main reasons for this increase, and to what extent did it arise from 
normal certification and billing cycles rather than delays in customer 
acceptance or certification?

As disclosed by the company, the group is supported by a healthy pipeline of projects. 
The group’s order book stood at $106.2 million as at 30 June 2026, with the majority 
comprising commercial projects, which are generally expected to be fulfilled over the next 
two years. 
 
On 16 January 2026, SGX RegCo issued a Regulator’s Column1 on forward guidance, in which 
the regulator strongly encouraged issuers to provide meaningful forward-looking 
disclosures. 
 
The Regulator’s Column can be accessed here: 
https://www.sgxgroup.com/media-centre/20260116-regulators-column-forward-

(i) 
Given SGX RegCo’s encouragement of forward guidance and its view that 
such disclosures can enhance investor confidence and credibility, has the 
board considered providing forward guidance for FY26/27 on the group’s 
performance, outlook, key operating assumptions, and strategic priorities? 
If not, why not? 
 
 
1 SGX RegCo noted that forward-looking information consistently ranks highly among the information

For the financial year ended 30 June 2026, revenue increased by 13.3% to $87.4 million, 
while employee benefits expense increased at a faster rate of 15.7% to $50.9 million.  
 
(Source: company annual report; emphasis added) 
 
Employee benefits expense accounted for approximately 58% of revenue in FY2026, a 
significant component of the group’s cost base. 
 
(i) 
Can management explain the key drivers of the increase in employee costs, 
including changes in headcount, remuneration and staffing requirements? 
What measure is the group taking to improve employee productivity and 
achieve operating leverage as the business scales? 
 
A milestone of FY2026 is the award of tender by ALPS for the provision of mobile inpatient 
care at home services to participating public healthcare institutions under the master service 
agreement.   
 
(ii) 
Can management provide shareholders with a clearer view of the 
addressable market for the group's mobile inpatient care services in 
Singapore? Does management consider the group to have a leading position 
in this market today? What are the group's principal competitive 
advantages, and how difficult would it be for competitors and new entrants 
to replicate its service model?

The group rationalised parts of its specialist clinic portfolio. Evoque Medical Aesthetics 
ceased operations with effect from 1 August 2026, while the Ho Kok Sun Colorectal 1 
specialist clinic and Lim Jit Fong Colorectal Centre ceased operations with effect from 1 July 
2026. Both colorectal clinics were acquired in full in 2014, and their operations have now 
ceased following the expiry of their respective clinic management service agreements on 30 
June 2026. Evoque was established by the group in 2023.  
 
At the same time, the group expanded its specialist care platform during the financial year, 
including the opening of its second orthopaedic clinic under Elite Orthopaedics and the 
inauguration of a new Breast & General Surgery clinic. 
 
(i) 
Can management confirm that the group no longer operates any colorectal 
specialist clinics following the expiry of the clinic management service 
agreements? Have the two colorectal specialists ceased practising with the 
group, or do they continue to have other roles or relationships with the 
group? 
 
(ii) 
Which specialist areas does the group intend to start or grow over the next 
three to five years, and will growth come primarily through establishing 
new clinics and recruiting additional specialists or via acquisitions? 
 
(iii) 
Given that specialist clinics acquired in 2014 have now ceased operations, 
does the board still regard acquiring clinics and their associated doctors as 
a sustainable growth model?

Cash and cash equivalents increased from approximately $16.4 million as at 30 June

At the group level, with cash and cash equivalents exceeding loans and borrowing (including

qa.question:
As disclosed in the annual report by both the chairman and CEO, management has set a 
target to double revenue by FY2031, while maintaining gross profit margin above 50% and 
keeping overhead costs below 20% of revenue. 
 
(i) 
What revenue contribution does management expect from the group’s core 
back-end consumable tooling business versus its high-precision build-to-
print component manufacturing business serving front-end wafer fab 
equipment (WFE) in order to achieve the FY2031 revenue target? What are 
the key assumptions for growth in each segment? 
 
(ii) 
Given the cyclical nature of the semiconductor industry and the significant 
investment associated with AI infrastructure, what assumptions does 
management make about semiconductor demand and the WFE cycle 
through FY2031? Does the board see any significant risk of the industry 
entering a downcycle in the near term, and how would this affect the group’s 
growth and investment plans? 
 
(iii) 
To what extent does the group’s FY2031 growth plan depend on 
acquisitions, particularly in the WFE segment? What capabilities, 
technologies or geographic markets, if any, would management seek to 
acquire?

The company will report a new segment, “Build-to-print Precision Components”, 
starting in FY2027.  
 
(Source: company annual report) 

Until FY2024, the group reported its segments on a geographical basis. Following a change 
in its internal reporting for decision-making and performance analysis, the group revised its 
reportable segments in accordance with SFRS(I) 8, Operating Segments. In FY2025 and 
FY2026, the group has reported three segments: Consumable Tools, WFE Parts, and 
Corporate and Others. 
 
(i) 
Can the board or audit & risk Committee (ARC) help shareholders better 
understand whether the new “Build-to-print Precision Components” 
segment is principally a reclassification of the existing WFE Parts business, 
or whether it represents an expansion or reorganisation of the business? 
What has changed in the underlying activities, customer base, capabilities, 
strategic positioning or management structure? 
 
(ii) 
How much of the group’s core capabilities in consumable tooling are 
transferable to the manufacture of precision components for WFE, and what 
additional manufacturing capabilities, processes, technology or expertise 
does the group need to develop to compete effectively in this market? 
 
While the group did not report any customer contributing more than 10% of total group’s 
revenue this year, it identified a major customer in the WFE segment contributing 
approximately $6.2 million to $6.3 million in revenue in each of the past two financial years.  
 
(iii) 
Can management help shareholders understand where MMUS sits in the 
WFE supply chain today, including whether it supplies directly to OEMs, 
contract manufacturers or other Tier 1 suppliers? Is MMUS itself qualified 
as a Tier 1 supplier to any major WFE customers, and how does the group 
intend to leverage its current position to identify, qualify for and win more 
large WFE customers?
qa.answer:
The Group does not provide segment-level revenue forecasts. Within Consumable Tools, it sees 
opportunities in advanced packaging and localisation, particularly in China, Malaysia, and Taiwan. 
For Build-to-Print Precision Components (“Build-to-Print”), the opportunity is supported by the much 
larger WFE market. At the same time, the Group sees opportunities brought by the convergence of 
front-end and back-end requirements. 
 
While the pace and mix will depend on market conditions, the Group believes its products, know-
how, team and global footprint position it well for the industry’s next phase of growth.

qa.question:
Total capital expenditure for FY2026 amounted to $3.8 million, of which $3.0 million 
was for plant and equipment, with the majority relating to the WFE segment.  
 
The CEO has disclosed that the group expects to invest $12.0 million in FY2027 to support 
its five-year plan, including expanding operations in markets where the group’s customers 
are growing and investing in next-generation processes and smarter manufacturing. 
 
This represents a significant increase in capital expenditure compared with $1.2 million in 
FY2025 and $2.0 million in FY2024. 
 
(i) 
Can management provide a breakdown of the planned $12.0 million of 
FY2027 capital expenditure between the consumable tools and WFE 
businesses? 
 
(ii) 
How much of the planned FY2027 capital expenditure is already supported 
by committed customer orders, contracts or capacity requirements, and 
how much is intended to build capacity ahead of anticipated demand?  

The group reported an earnings per share of 11.44 cents for FY2026 and paid a dividend of 
6 cents per share. The reported payout ratio was 52.4%, compared with 67.3% previously, 
while the group’s dividend policy is to pay out at least 40% of net audited profit. Total 
dividends for FY2026 amounted to $8.3 million. 
 
(iii) 
With FY2027 capital expenditure expected to increase significantly, can the 
group fund its planned growth investments while maintaining the current 
6-cent dividend? What factors does the board consider in determining 
whether the 6-cent dividend can be sustained, and what gives the board

qa.answer:
The Group does not assume that demand will be linear through FY2031. However, over the long 
term, the Group believes the industry will continue to grow as semiconductors become increasingly 
important across a wider range of applications.  
 
The Group therefore believes that strategic investment through the industry cycle is key to 
enhancing its long-term competitive position. This provides the flexibility to capture opportunities, 
stay resilient, and continue progressing towards its FY2031 growth objectives. 
 
4. To what extent does the Group’s FY2031 growth plan depend on acquisitions, particularly 
in the Build-to-Print segment? What capabilities, technologies or geographic markets, if any, 
would management seek to acquire? 
The Group’s mid-term growth strategy focuses mainly on organic growth across three key priorities. 
The first is strengthening customer support through expanded operations and localised capabilities. 
The Group will strengthen its presence across key semiconductor markets to provide faster and 
more effective customer support. This includes expanding operations in China and Malaysia, where 
customers and the industry continue to grow, and building a stronger physical presence in Taiwan. 
The second is next-generation processing. The Group will invest in next-generation equipment and 
processes to enhance its capabilities in process-critical applications. 
The third is smart and secure manufacturing. The Group will increase the use of data-driven 
decision-making to improve operational effectiveness and support long-term innovation, while 
developing ISO 27001-aligned cybersecurity capabilities to strengthen its position as a trusted 
supplier of choice. 
The Group also remains open to acquisitions that can support these areas of its strategy, with its 
strong financial position providing the flexibility to act when suitable opportunities arise. 
 
B. Operations 
 
5. Decentralised operations depend on strong local decision-makers, and the share scheme 
appears designed to align managers’ interests with shareholders. With the COO and CFO 
retiring and the CEO stepping back to become Chairman, has responsibility shifted to the 
local management teams or become more concentrated at the top? 
The Group’s decentralised structure allows it to stay responsive to customers and provide quick 
local support with consistent, high-quality service. The Group takes a hands-on approach to 
management, working closely with teams on the ground to understand challenges and improve 
execution. 
The Five-Star Factory initiative helps bring this together by giving teams around the world a 
common framework for learning, sharing ideas and solving problems together. 
As part of its focus to build High Performance Teams, the Group continues to recruit and develop 
talent across all levels and locations, strengthening local support for customers worldwide.  
 
 

6. The Group will report a new segment, “Build-to-Print Precision Components”, starting in 
FY2027. Is the new segment principally a reclassification of the existing WFE parts business, 
or is it an expansion or reorganisation of the business? What has changed in the underlying 
activities, customer base, capabilities, strategic positioning or management structure? 
 
The change relates only to the segment descriptions and naming convention. It is intended to better 
reflect how the Group creates value for its customers, aligning segment reporting with its 
competitive positioning and strategic direction rather than the end-market served. There is no 
change to the Group’s underlying operations, management structure or reportable segments. 
 
7. How much of the Group’s core capabilities in consumable tooling are transferable to the 
manufacture of precision components for WFE, and what additional manufacturing 
capabilities, processes, technology or expertise does the Group need to develop to compete 
effectively in this market? 
The Group’s core capabilities are highly transferable across both business segments, as 
Consumable Tools and Build-to-Print parts require the same commitment to precision engineering, 
process control, quality, reliability and continuous improvement. The Group also benefits from a 
culture of sharing technical knowledge, lessons learned, and best practices across its operations, 
supported by the common framework of its Five-Star Factory initiative.  
As parts become more complex and customer requirements more demanding, the Group continues 
to invest in its process, quality and engineering capabilities to remain a trusted supplier of choice. 
In FY2026, these investments included a new machine to improve machining quality and efficiency, 
as well as a physics-based programming technology that can increase material removal rates by 
10-30% for long-cycle parts. With its mid-term growth strategy, the Group is also using data to 
improve operations and innovation, while strengthening cybersecurity in line with ISO 27001 
requirements. 
 
8. Where does MMUS sit in the WFE supply chain today, including whether it supplies directly 
to OEMs, contract manufacturers or other Tier 1 suppliers? Is MMUS itself qualified as a Tier 
1 supplier to any major WFE customers? How does the Group intend to leverage its current 
position to identify, qualify for and win larger WFE customers? 
MMUS mainly serves the Build-to-Print segment, supplying critical build-to-print precision 
components to WFE customers and other high-tech industries globally. Its parts are used in areas 
such as deposition and etch applications.  
As a Next Generation Supplier, its value lies in manufacturing difficult parts accurately, consistently 
and efficiently. The Group continues to engage customers to better understand and solve their 
problems, strengthen its engineering and manufacturing processes, and improve its factories 
through the Five-Star Factory initiative. This is increasingly important as semiconductor 
manufacturing becomes more complex and customers place greater emphasis on supplier 
capability and reliability. By consistently meeting these requirements, the Group believes the Build-
to-Print business can win more critical work over time. 
 
 

C. Financials 
 
9. Was the inventory write-off in FY2026 due to obsolescence (overproduction or unsaleable)? 
What is the typical average lead time before inventory goes obsolete? 
Inventory write-offs for FY2026 were S$73k, compared with S$166k in FY2025. Obsolescence risk 
varies by product, as customer requirements, part numbers and product programmes can change 
quickly. Under its Five-Star Factory initiative, the Group continues to improve the way it plans and 
manages inventory, while working to shorten lead times and deliver on time. 
 
10. Inventory stood at 6.5% of sales for FY2026 versus 4.8% of sales in the previous financial 
year. Is there a fixed threshold on this? 
With higher material costs and longer lead times, the Group built up inventory to fulfil confirmed 
backlog orders. 
While there is no fixed threshold for inventory, the Group remains disciplined in managing inventory 
levels and minimising obsolescence risk. This is especially important for the Consumable Tools 
segment, where customers’ requirements can change quickly as they seek to improve yields, cycle 
times and efficiency.
 
11. Can management provide a breakdown of the planned S$12.0 million of FY2027 capital 
expenditure between the Consumable Tools and Build-to-Print businesses? How much of 
the planned FY2027 capital expenditure is already supported by committed customer orders, 
contracts or capacity requirements, and how much is intended to build capacity ahead of 
anticipated demand? 
The Group does not disclose the breakdown the S$12.0 million investment by segment, or by 
committed versus anticipated demand. The investment is intended to support the three priority 
areas of its mid-term strategy: expanding operations and local capabilities, building next-generation 
processing capabilities, and advancing smart and secure manufacturing. 
The Group reviews its capital expenditure plans every six months to stay responsive to changing 
customer needs. This helps the Group invest with discipline and add capacity where it sees 
sustainable, long-term demand rather than reacting to short-term changes in the cycle. 
 
12. With FY2027 capital expenditure expected to increase significantly, can the Group fund its 
planned growth investments while maintaining the current 6-cent dividend? What factors 
does the Board consider in determining whether the 6-cent dividend can be sustained, and 
what gives the Board confidence that the higher investment programme will not come at the 
expense of shareholder distributions? 
For FY2026, total dividends represented a payout ratio of 52.4%. This exceeded the Group’s 
practice of distributing at least 40% of after-tax annual earnings, after considering financial 
performance, projected cash flow, capital requirements for business growth, and economic or other 
conditions. 
The Group remains focused on balancing long-term growth with sustainable shareholder returns. 
This means being thoughtful and disciplined about how capital is used, while ensuring that it does 
not limit good growth opportunities. The Group will continue this approach as it executes its mid-
term strategy, taking into consideration cash flow and investment needs.
